reading.rtitle: Say the Line Before the Room Does
paras: In almost every credit meeting there is a moment when a chart goes on the screen and the room goes quiet. Everybody looks at the line, and then everybody looks at the person who owns it. What happens in the next ten seconds tells the room more about that person than the chart does.

People who sound junior describe the chart point by point: January was three point one, February was two point nine, March was three point one. All of it is correct, and none of it helps, because the room can read numbers. People who sound senior describe the shape first. The rate was flat for a quarter, it rose sharply in April, it peaked in May, and it is falling again.

The shape is only half of the sentence. The other half is the speed and the size. A rise of one point over a year and a rise of one point in a month are different stories, and the words sharply and gradually are how the room hears the difference. The numbers come last, and only two of them: where it started and where it ended, or the difference between them.

Then comes the part most people forget, which is the reason. A line that went up needs a because, and a line that came down needs one too, or somebody will ask for it. The best presenters answer the question before it is asked. They say what the line did, how fast, why, and what they expect next, and then they stop.
reading.source: A composite of advice given to analysts who present data, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how to build a chart in a spreadsheet so that the numbers are easy to read for everybody in a meeting.
To show how senior people describe a chart: shape, speed, numbers, and reason.
To argue that charts are less useful than tables in credit meetings.

listenings.text: Let me describe the approval rate, because it is the line everybody is asking about. In January, February and March it was flat, at around sixty percent. Nothing moved. In April there was a small dip, to fifty-eight, and that was the first signal. Then the new rule came in at the end of April, and in May approvals fell sharply, by eight points, to fifty-two percent. That was expected. In June the rate rose slightly, to fifty-four. So it has started to recover, but slowly. For the next quarter, we expect approvals to recover gradually and to level off at about fifty-six percent. We do not expect them to go back to sixty, and that is a decision, not a problem.

I ask three questions of every chart I see, and most charts fail at least one of them. The first question is about the axis. Where does it start? If the axis starts at ninety-five instead of zero, a rise of two points looks like a mountain. It is the oldest trick there is, and it still works. The second question is about the start date. Why does the line begin here? If you start a chart at the lowest point of the year, every line looks like a recovery. Somebody chose that date, and you should ask why. The third question is the most important one: compared with what? A rate that rose by two points means nothing on its own. Compared with last year, with the market, or with the plan? Without a comparison, a number is just a number, and a chart is just a picture.
